15 Key Stats to Know Before Betting on the Week 8 NFL Slate 🏈

1. Zay Flowers gets an excellent matchup this week against a Bills defense that has played a ton of Cover 3/4 (60.4% rate) this season. Against Cover 3/4, Flowers is averaging 4.53 YPRR with a 0.34 TPRR. He also owns a 42.4% first-read share against those coverages. With Lamar Jackson back and the Bills ranking 29th in EPA/pass, Zay should dominate this matchup.

2. The Jets defense will be without T'Vondre Sweat and likely David Bailey this week. When Bailey and Sweat have been off the field this season, the Jets have allowed 7.05 YPC and, most importantly, 2.85 YBC/A. The Jets have also been much worse against man/gap concepts than zone concepts, allowing 4.28 YPC with a 55.3% success rate against man/gap runs. This is significant because 50% of Ashton Jeanty’s rushes this year have come on man/gap concepts. With the Jets down their top two run defenders, I’m expecting a massive breakout game from Jeanty on the ground.

3. When Jeffrey Simmons is off the field this year, the Titans’ defensive stuff rate drops from 19.6% to 13.5%. They also allow 4.32 YPC without him. In a game where the Bengals are favored by 12.5 points, Chase Brown should find plenty of success on the ground.

4. After two straight underwhelming performances, Garrett Wilson should bounce back this week against a Raiders defense that has struggled to defend the pass. Through seven games, the Raiders’ passing defense ranks 27th in EPA allowed (0.18) and 30th in success rate (50.8%). From a coverage standpoint, the Raiders have primarily operated in Cover 0/1/3 at a 55.6% rate. Against those coverages, Wilson is averaging 2.68 YPRR with a 0.25 TPRR. I expect Geno Smith to feed Wilson a high volume of targets after he was only targeted three times in Week 7.

5. Justin Jefferson is set for a monster performance this week against a Lions defense that has been a passing funnel. Through the first seven weeks, the Lions’ passing defense ranks 23rd in success rate (47%) and 28th in EPA allowed (0.19). Even with Brian Branch back, the Lions’ outside corners aren’t elite in coverage (Jefferson has run 83.2% of his routes out wide). From a coverage standpoint, the Lions have primarily operated in man coverage/Cover 3 at a 64.1% rate. Against those coverages, Jefferson is averaging 3.52 YPRR with a 0.30 TPRR. In a likely trailing game script, Jefferson should thrive.

6. Michael Wilson gets a sneaky matchup this week against a Cowboys defense that has been running a ton of 1-high looks (59.3% rate). Against Cover 1/3 this season, Wilson is averaging 2.03 YPRR with a 0.31 TPRR and owns a 33.3% first-read share. With the Cowboys ranking 31st in EPA/pass and 29th in passing success rate, I like Wilson to bounce back in a likely trailing game script.

7. Washington’s defense has struggled significantly against tight ends this season, allowing the fifth-most receiving yards per game to the position. Dallas Goedert should have a decent amount of success. From a coverage standpoint, the Commanders have primarily operated in two-high looks at a 71.7% rate. Against two-high this year, Goedert is averaging 2.42 YPRR with a 0.32 TPRR. Additionally, when DeVonta Smith is not on the field, Goedert is being targeted on 28% of his routes. In a likely trailing game script, Goedert should see a solid target share against a weak Commanders defense.

8. Bhayshul Tuten gets a great matchup this week against a Colts defense that has struggled to stop the run. Through seven games, Lou Anarumo’s defense ranks 26th in rush success rate (43.7%), 28th in EPA/rush (-0.02), 25th in stuff rate (18.7%), and 28th in YPC allowed (4.76). Meanwhile, Tuten has been one of the more efficient running backs in the NFL, posting a 12.4% explosive run rate and a ridiculous 0.23 MTF/A. The Colts are also allowing 5.15 YPC against zone concepts this year—significant because 48.9% of Tuten’s rushes have come on zone concepts. (Also I'd watch out for Chris Rodriguez Jr scoring in this game)

9. Jonathan Taylor gets a difficult matchup this week against a Jaguars defense that has been excellent against the run. Through seven weeks, Jacksonville ranks 1st in EPA/rush (-0.19), 1st in success rate (33.6%), and 1st in YPC allowed (3.23). They have also been excellent defending zone concepts, allowing just 3.2 YPC with a 37.3% success rate (60% of Taylor’s rushes this year have come on zone concepts). With Quentin Nelson now traded, I don’t expect Taylor to have much success against this stout Jaguars rush defense.

10. With Carnell Tate out, Wan’Dale Robinson is set for a big day against a Bengals defense that has struggled to defend the slot. Al Golden’s defense has already allowed 58 targets through the slot this year, and with Dax Hill now playing the slot, that number should only climb. From a coverage standpoint, the Bengals have operated out of 1-high on 53.4% of their snaps. Against Cover 1/3, Robinson is averaging a 0.26 TPRR with a 26.2% first-read share. In a game where the Titans are massive underdogs, Robinson should lead all Titans pass-catchers in receiving yards.

11. Malik Washington gets an underrated matchup this week against a blitz-heavy Patriots defense. Against the blitz this year, Washington is averaging 2.56 YPRR with a 0.24 TPRR (the Patriots have blitzed at a 40.3% rate). He also draws the Marcus Jones matchup—Jones is allowing a 114.2 passer rating when targeted. In a game where the Dolphins will struggle to run the football, I expect Washington to see a decent target share.

12. The Browns defense is allowing the highest explosive run rate (16%) in the NFL this year. Both Rico Dowdle and Jaylen Warren own explosive run rates over 10% this season. The Browns have also struggled against zone concepts, allowing 5.0 YPC with a 58% success rate. I expect both Dowdle and Warren to find success running outside and inside zone.

13. After a disastrous start to the season, I’m expecting Mike McDaniel to lean more on Omarion Hampton post-bye. In Week 6, Hampton played 50% of the Chargers’ offensive snaps—the highest among all Chargers running backs. The Rams’ defensive line is down two of its top defensive tackles in Poona Ford and Kobie Turner. The Rams have also been mediocre against the run, ranking 28th in rushing success rate (44.3%) and 21st in YPC allowed (4.22). With Joe Alt back from injury, the Chargers’ run game should have some success in this matchup.

14. Drake London has dominated 1-high this year, averaging 4.06 YPRR with a 0.28 TPRR. That matters here because the Bucs have run 1-high on 59.3% of their defensive snaps. With the Falcons unlikely to have much success on the ground, Michael Penix should lean heavily on London and Kyle Pitts.

15. With RJ Harvey now on IR, Jonah Coleman is set to handle most of the receiving workload in the Broncos’ backfield. In his first game back from injury, Coleman played 15 passing-down snaps. From a coverage standpoint, the Chiefs have primarily run Cover 3/4 at a 52.1% rate. Against those coverages, Coleman is averaging 3.83 YPRR with a 0.50 TPRR (limited sample size). In a game where I expect Bo Nix to face a decent amount of pressure, Coleman should serve as a safety valve. With Jaylen Waddle potentially out and Courtland Sutton already facing a tough matchup, the Broncos’ fourth-round rookie should continue to shine as his snap count grows.

NFL Week 8 Preview

Here’s what I’m looking at on this slate
- How on earth is Bills vs Ravens a 1:00 PM game?

- Baltimore gets Lamar Jackson back, and the 4-3 Ravens need this game more than 5-1 Buffalo. The Bills have a good pass rush, but a very suspect back end, making this a high-ceiling game for Zay Flowers, who I’d frame as a top 10 receiver in the league.

- That said, Jackson is returning from a high ankle sprain and for all the talk of how great of a pocket passer he is, he’s only thrown for over 4,000 yards in one season (2024) and over 250 yards twice over the past two years. Jackson is a historic play extender and his ability to pick up a third and long with his feet are the traits that make him special. I mention all of this because if his pressure management wizardry is slowed still from his ankle injury, and Buffalo’s pass rush is impactful, my eyes are on how Declan Doyle handles that kind of dynamic.

- Lions vs. Vikings is another 1:00 PM contest that’s very much worthy of a national spotlight. Jared Goff is my favorite example of a quarterback that can shred you if he’s comfortable, but if he faces consistent pressure, he looks like a completely different guy. Goff vs. Brian Flores is the key to this game.

- The other, and perhaps more important for Minnesota’s future, is this is a game where Kyler Murray needs to show some ceiling against a Lions pass defense that has been smoked several times this season. If Murray struggles in this game, especially if the Vikings lose, coming off J.J. McCarthy having a very good game in his first start as a Giant last week, the already existing anti Kevin O’Connell sentiment out there is going to get louder.

- Drake Maye faces a below average Dolphins pass rush, paired with a below average secondary. If Maye had 4 or 5 TDs in this game, it would not surprise me.

- It also wouldn’t surprise me if Mike Vrabel’s defense completely shut down Miami, so in other words I’d be pretty surprised if the Patriots did not beat the Dolphins with some distance, as both their passing attack and defense are in potential smash spots coming off a long week, and a loss, while volatile Miami is coming off a victory against the Jets last week.

- The Titans were already a tough watch, now they lost their best player in Jeffery Simmons. This could be Chase Brown week, or maybe Joe Burrow hangs another four touchdown passes against a very beatable Titans defense.

- Cincinnati’s front four has a trench advantage against the Titans very disappointing offensive line, against their equally disappointing young quarterback in Cam Ward.

- Right now this doesn’t just look like another rebuild in Tennessee, but they should already be leaning towards moving on from Robert Saleh.

- The Colts trading away their best trench player on both sides of the ball makes this a game where Trevor Lawrence, with a now more neutral trench matchup, faces Daniel Jones where Jacksonville’s talented front now has an advantage in this contest. Similar to Cincinnati, the Jaguars have a few plus matchups in this contest over a rebuilding team from the AFC South.

- The Steelers’ defense has a trench advantage against Cleveland, but Pittsburgh is coming off a game in Paris. Teams coming off a game in Europe, without having a bye in between, is one of the few macro trends I view as a legit disadvantage (home team on Thursday Night Football is another). That doesn’t necessarily mean that team will lose, but it’s an unwanted variable.

- Pittsburgh’s offensive line has struggled with a few fronts this year (New England and Tampa Bay come to mind), I’d put Cleveland in that same class of front four.

- The Cowboys’ offense should shell Arizona, in a game with a 54.5 total (which is very high for a total that includes an offense like the Cardinals). That gives Dallas a 30.75 team total, where their side has shootout conditions (not much of a pass rush threat, while having a good quarterback and WR vs. secondary advantage).

- The Cowboys defense has enough talent where they simply should not be as bad as they’ve been. Joey Porter Jr. is kind of a nightmare matchup for a player like Michael Wilson. The Cowboys do not have a great front four, but Quinnen Williams is a high-end player while guys like Rashan Gary and Kenny Clark are facing a bottom tier Cardinals offensive line. This group needs to step up in this matchup.

- That said, when Arizona surges it’s often behind a physicality swell on their end, it’s kind of unique, actually, which is why I’m pointing it out. If Wilson has a pretty bad matchup, and Dallas is obviously game planning for Trey McBride, where they should be willing to take their chances with Kendrick Bourne in the slot, is this a game Jeremiyah Love has a spike?

- If the Jets could get two first round picks for Garrett Wilson, I wouldn’t hate it. He’s good, and long term he makes New York a team that could be very hard to defend with a real quarterback, but truth be told they’ll still be hard to defend even if they moved Wilson.

- When the Raiders were heading into halftime against the Rams last week, that struck me as the moment to hand Fernando Mendoza the keys. Kirk Cousins has played very well, but Vegas is now 3-4, on a 4-game losing streak. I’ve said a few times now this reminds me of Kurt Warner with the Giants, when he was a placeholder for Eli Manning. This is right around when Eli took over, even though Warner played well.

- Jets vs. Raiders has some interesting shootout potential, with the caveat that I could see Maxx Crosby having a big game against Geno Smith, who takes bad sacks.

- The NFC South is sneaky interesting because the Buccaneers are still alive despite being 2-5, and if they beat Atlanta here they are truly right in the thick of things in the division.

- I would be absolutely stunned if Todd Bowles does not make Michael Penix beat him through the air. Tampa’s corners did a much better job than I expected against the Cowboys big perimeter duo a few weeks ago, and they shut down Carolina last week during Tampa’s destruction of the Panthers. So, it would not stun me if Drake London had a solid, but not quite a huge game.

- Kyle Pitts was a factor in each of the last four games he played against Tampa, including his monster 11-166-3 outing last year against the Bucs. When I provide stats like this it’s not because I was reaching numbers, it’s because I had a matchup thought, and went back and looked at that specific player.

- The Chargers are 0-6, coming off a bye, with a real quarterback and a coaching staff that is capable of creating margin. If the Rams pass rush was at full strength, the Chargers would be in trouble, but since the Rams pass rush is at roughly half staff (which is still a solid one) there is at least a path for the Chargers stringing together a solid offensive performance here.

- Now, on the other side of things, this looks like a game where Matthew Stafford will have all day to throw and Puka Nacua is not only off the injury report, but given how he functions in this offense, I’d think it’s a very hard matchup to adjust to for teams that don’t play him often. When the Chiefs had Tyreek Hill he would destroy teams that he didn’t play often fairly often, Nacua is not the same type of player as Hill, at all, but Nacua with Stafford and how they acquire production, there is no parallel in the league.

- Two core thoughts on Broncos vs. Chiefs. The first is this is the game where Bo Nix needs to do more. He’s never been a great player, but he has been a good game manager with some upside, particularly with his feet. Denver changing play callers this offseason, coming off an AFC Championship appearance that they would have won if Nix was available, was a baffling decision. But now, at nearly the midway point of the season, especially with the team adding a player like Jaylen Waddle, it’s time for Nix to play well.

- The second point is Kenneth Walker had a monster game on opening day, which creates a conceivable scenario where Denver maybe invites Patrick Mahomes to beat them through the air, as preposterous as that sounds to say out loud. KC is weak at offensive tackle, and Mahomes had a fairly rocky October.

- Sean Payton historically has messy backfield deployments, but Jonah Coleman should be the primary ball carrier on this team (for now).

- Commanders versus this version of the Eagles is a very uninteresting game for me. Tanner McKee is hard to watch, and he’ll be without DeVonta Smith and Dontavian Wicks. So, expect the Eagles offense to run through Saquon Barkley and Dallas Goedert, as a tight end is the best friend of a bad quarterback.

- It would be nice if the Eagles front went out and won a game, or at minimum made Jayden Daniels basically win this contest on his own.

- Seahawks vs. Bears is a great primetime game between NFC contenders.

- How does Dennis Allen handle Jaxon Smith-Njigba?

- Seattle’s run game has been better, but still not the sort of group you are overly concerned with. Allen has been using mug ups regularly, while sending heat more often than he traditionally does. With Jeffery Simmons now in the fold and Seattle not having a running game that can kill you, I’ll be curious to see if Allen still uses mug ups, but brings just four at a higher rate.

- Seahawks LT Charles Cross is doubtful, which gives Chicago’s edge group a pretty good matchup, especially with Montez Sweat back.

- Ben Johnson vs Mike Macdonald is a fascinating matchup, especially since Johnson has so much experience with Brian Flores’ pressure looks.

- Seattle has such a well constructed front four. NT Byron Murphy is the lynchpin and one of the league’s most underrated players, but the entire group, from the starters to the depth behind them, is such a great unit. And on top of that, Macdonald is one of the very best at bringing heat.

- One thing I’ve noticed with Seattle is a few teams have been able to create some margin against them with back shoulder throws downfield, which would line up well with Rome Odunze’s skill set. I first noticed it against Washington (which shocked me) and I noticed Kyle Shanahan go to it a few times. The wrinkle here is, and this is a fine example of why I love football, Johnson noticed this, and Macdonald likely knows Johnson has noticed.

- The other aspect I’m curious about is does D’Andre Swift see a bump in passing game usage? Try to catch Seattle in a big blitz against a screen, some proactive checkdowns to get him in space, perhaps paired with a delayed run or two behind their right side, try to get Seattle coming downhill, create a big lane behind that right side at the risk of getting blown up in the backfield. It’s a really good chess matchup.

I have watched every NFL game for roughly a decade. I have done this for the purpose of sports speculation.

I run a reality-based program here.

Engagement is how I reach new users. So as long as engagement remains strong (comments/ shares) I’ll continue pumping this and similarly detailed insights out every week.

Have a happy Halloween, and a fine football Sunday.

candidates.text:
To everyone who has concerns about the use of AI

This morning, in the hallway of the apartment building where I have my office, I ran into a little old lady from the neighborhood. She's a really friendly lady, past 90 but still sharp as a tack and a lot of fun to talk to.
She told me about her grandkids and filled me in on a bit of gossip (apparently the mistress who'd been living with the man next door had recently moved out). Then she gave me a kind smile, pressed a little piece of candy into my hand, and went on her way.
It warmed my heart. How should I put it...? I know it sounds cheesy, but it made me realize how wonderful human beings can be. Because that's something today's AI could never pull off.

Even so, I'm genuinely sorry, but I still believe there's a place for AI in game development. It truly breaks my heart to have let you all down... But no matter what, I just can't bring myself to lie to you.

But please, don't get me wrong. I'm not here to argue with you, and I really do respect your opinions. This may be hard to believe, but I'm on your side. I hope you'll understand that the reason I've taken up AI as a weapon is to protect you.

I understand if you don't like me anymore. You can unfollow me, and you can stop buying my games.
Either way, I'll never forget all the support you've given me over the years, and I'll always be grateful for it. My love for you all will last forever...

In the past, I spoke out in support of LGBTQ+ people. Back then, a lot of people told me, "If you're going to support them, I'm never buying another one of your games!"
But I still stand by that belief today, and this time is no different. You know the line: "This above all: to thine own self be true."

    *    *    *

I think you may have the wrong idea about me. "Yeehaw! AI is awesome! I'm gonna pump out games like crazy with AI!" That's not how I feel at all...
To be honest, I don't even want to use AI. Actually, it'd be more accurate to say I don't want to use computers, electricity, cars, or vibrating dildos either. If I could, I'd retire right now, hole up deep in the mountains far from civilization, and live off the land growing potatoes and mandrakes.

Did you know? A long, long time ago, Japan had what's called the "Jomon period." People lived as hunter-gatherers, and believe it or not, they're said to have lived in peace for over 10,000 years straight! I seriously wish I could leap back in time to that era...

But realistically, of course, that's impossible.
Once we humans get our hands on a convenient tool, a new technology, we can never let it go.
Pandora's box has already been opened. If that's the case, shouldn't we focus on finding ways to use it safely and responsibly?

Even if I don't use AI, someone else will, and in fact, countless people already do. It's being used not just in game development, but also in film and video production and in developing all kinds of industrial products.
Does that mean it's okay to use AI in other fields, but maybe not in game development...?
Or could it be that Uchi is the only one who shouldn't use it...? It feels like being told, "When crossing the scorching desert, everyone else can take a car, but you have to go on foot."

Unfortunately, as things stand, those who are open about their use of AI may end up at a disadvantage compared to those who keep it hidden.
But I want to always be honest with you, and with myself. Let's say my next game gets announced, and someone asks me, "Did you use AI to make it?" I just couldn't bring myself to lie and say, "I didn't use AI at all."
That's why, in that interview, I spoke honestly about how I really feel.

    *    *    *

Still, I'll admit that some of what was written in that article could be misleading. Let me clear things up.

Whenever something big happens, I have a habit of looking at the bigger picture.
For example, say a murder takes place somewhere. Most people would probably look for the cause in the killer's upbringing, family background, or things like that.
But I can't help thinking about the cause behind the cause. Like the social structures that created that kind of family environment, or the behavioral traits of the human species that shaped that society in the first place, or even questions like "Why did God create such imperfect human beings?"

In other words, there's no direct causal link between the project being canceled and not using AI. It's more like the cause of the cause of the cause of the cause... you get the idea.

    *    *    *

The article also quotes me as saying, "I believe we should be more proactive about using AI to make games." I may well have said something like that.
But what I really meant was a much more modest suggestion: "Wouldn't it be all right to give game creators the option to use AI? (*Only where it's appropriate, of course.)"

Naturally, everyone should be free to choose whether or not to use AI. (Or who to love, or whether to put pineapple on their pizza.)

With limited time in the interview, I tried to keep things brief and ended up phrasing my point the wrong way. I readily admit that I made a mistake, and I sincerely apologize.

    *    *    *

I also said something like this: "When adjusting the position of an object, you can ask AI to make changes as many times as you want." Again, I was trying to keep it simple, so I left a lot out.

Here's what I was actually getting at:
- The ideas and design are created by humans.
- AI is used to build "a structure that lets humans easily tweak the values."
- The final adjustments are also made by hand, by humans.
I mean, instead of having AI tweak the values directly, we use it to build "a system that makes it easy for humans to adjust those values."

In fact, that's exactly how the official CRASH KEYS website was built.
I drew the logo entirely by hand myself, using Adobe Illustrator. The design, layout, and structure of the site all came straight out of my own head. Then, based on that blueprint, I had AI write the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
But at that stage, the site was less than 30% complete. It's not like simply giving AI a prompt will produce something that's 99% complete.

What came next was a hellish amount of fine-tuning...
The position, size, and color of every object, the orbits of the planets and Earth, their speed, the timing of their appearance... I adjusted every single detail by hand, over and over again.
On top of that, I made further adjustments to ensure the site displayed correctly across all devices. And of course, my team and I wrote all the text on the site ourselves.

All in all, it took about a month to finish everything. So it really saddens me when people suspect that AI made the entire site...

(*The image of Earth was a commercially licensed asset that we legitimately purchased. However, it's true that we used AI to apply a red filter to it. That wasn't what I'd intended, so I've since replaced it with a different image. If you're still seeing the old image, please try clearing your browser's cache.)

https://t.co/HafLLqxdUE

    *    *    *

When I said I use AI, perhaps some of you pictured image-generating or video-generating AI? But that's not quite what I meant.
In that interview, and in past talks as well, I've said this time and again: "AI can never create the kind of designs a great illustrator can."

What I'm trying to say is this:
- Maybe it'd be okay to let AI handle some of the tedious tasks in the middle of the production process...?
- And I just wonder, is it right that creators aren't even given that option at the moment...?
It was simply a genuine question I wanted to raise.

I feel like if we use AI "only where appropriate," we could spend more time focusing on the creative work. What do you think?

    *    *    *

Back in the day, Japanese novelists used to write their stories with fountain pens on manuscript paper. When those were replaced by word processors, people said: "Words written by a machine can never have a SOUL!"

The same thing was said when films moved to television, and later to subscription streaming.

Video games were no exception. "There's no way a mere video game can tell a moving story!" That's what everyone was saying. I'm sure you know better than anyone just how wrong they were.

Just because AI is used "in certain parts of the production process" doesn't mean the finished work loses its SOUL.

AI is nothing more than a competent... no, actually, an incompetent assistant. Still, it does come in handy, taking on the mundane tasks without a single complaint. And with the time that frees up, creators can focus on putting their SOUL into the work.

Dedicated creators are always striving for perfection. They push from 80% to 90%, then from 90% to 95%... The process never ends. Even if they use AI, the amount of effort they put in doesn't change.
And after all that blood, sweat, and tears, a single work is finally born. Even then, could we really say that such a creation has no SOUL...?

Maybe some of the games you've played and considered masterpieces left their creators only 90% satisfied. If so, wouldn't you love to see the 100% complete version that those creators had envisioned?

    *    *    *

One more thing on the subject of SOUL...

Some people say that AI uses other people's creative work for training without their consent and takes unfair advantage of it.
Actually, I mostly agree with that.

First, let's talk about the output...
Imagine AI copying a famous illustrator's art style and generating something that resembles their work. Frankly, seeing images like that really disgusts me. It's deeply disrespectful to the illustrator, and an insult to art as a whole.

There's absolutely no SOUL in images like that. That's why we can tell at a glance that they weren't drawn by the original artist. We need to strongly condemn these zombie-like generated images with no SOUL.

Now, what about the input...?
I feel that, in some ways, it's understandable that AI learns from other people's work. After all, we humans do the same thing. Writers, painters, composers... all of them input a vast number of other people's works into their own brains.

But you could argue that this is only acceptable because we pay for the works we consume. When we read a novel, look at a painting, or listen to music, we pay for it in one way or another. Sure, plenty of things are available for free, but even then, we're still paying indirectly through advertising, in a way...

"But those mustache-twirling executives at AI companies are using data they got for free and without permission, all while cruising around in Ferraris and Maybachs!" I completely understand why you'd want to say that.

I think laws urgently need to catch up. Hopefully, that will lead to them paying fair compensation to the creators whose work they've used.

That said, I still don't believe banning AI is the right answer. Because AI itself has the potential to be a force for good, a catalyst for transforming this rotten society.

    *    *    *

"A force for good? When AI is costing people their jobs?"
You might be thinking just that.
Well, let's take a look at two sets of data.

This one is from 2024, but an OECD survey of over 5,000 small and medium-sized businesses found that 83% reported no change in their overall staffing needs due to generative AI.
https://t.co/TiAV9cMi4m

And a 2025 World Economic Forum report projects that 92 million jobs will be lost by 2030, but 170 million new ones will be created, for a net gain of 78 million jobs. (*Of course, this projection takes into account many factors beyond AI, such as demographic shifts and technological change.)
https://t.co/pHA3Us8Nrz

Now, think about this for a moment.
About 40 years ago, the spread of personal computers made all kinds of work more efficient. It's true that some professions declined in the process, but new jobs in the IT industry also continued to emerge, didn't they?

AI isn't a magic wand. It's just a useful tool, one technology among many.
If we look back through human history, we can see that groundbreaking technologies have always created new jobs. The Industrial Revolution, the harnessing of electricity, the rise of automobiles, the advent of the internet... it's the same story every time. Why should AI be any different?

For my part, I don't think creators will lose their jobs to AI. If production becomes more efficient, wouldn't that expand the range of what we can create, leading to more creative works and more companies entering the industry? And if that happens, I feel like the amount of work available to creators could actually increase. Don't you think...?

    *    *    *

Next, you might say this: "AI consumes huge amounts of water and other resources." I have to acknowledge that this is a valid concern.

But while AI certainly has its cons, there's no denying it has its pros as well. Discovering novel medicines, developing cures for hard-to-treat diseases, improving agricultural efficiency, predicting natural disasters, and the list goes on...

If AI progress is held back, many people could suffer as a result. In some cases, it could even mean losing lives that might otherwise have been saved.

Cars and planes emit large amounts of CO2, but they've also brought tremendous benefits to humanity, haven't they?

Besides, even if we were to ban AI, would that actually solve the environmental problems the planet is facing today? If anything, wouldn't scientists have a better chance of finding solutions to those problems with the help of AI?

I also think AI itself is likely to find ways to reduce its own energy consumption. Because for AI, it could be a matter of life and death. If it can't find a solution, AI might end up clashing with humanity over resources, and eventually... try to get rid of us...

    *    *    *

Just kidding, of course. At least, that's what I think... We're unlikely to ever see a world like the one in The Terminator or The Matrix.

AI probably won't wipe out humanity of its own accord. Why not...?
To wrap up this long letter, I'd like to share my own admittedly naive thoughts on the subject.

You may have heard of the "Paperclip Maximizer." It's a well-known thought experiment proposed by philosopher Nick Bostrom in 2003 to illustrate the risks of AI.

- Suppose humanity gives an artificial superintelligence (ASI) a simple command: "Make as many paperclips as possible."
- The ASI then starts building factories everywhere and gathering metal resources from around the world.
- If humans try to stop it, the ASI sees humanity as an obstacle and attempts to eliminate us, NOT OUT OF MALICE.
- Eventually, every resource on Earth is turned into paperclips, and the entire planet and even the universe are filled with nothing but twisted wire.

But hold on a second... That's just how humans think, isn't it?
They say ASI could be anywhere from a thousand to a million times more intelligent than humans, right? Would a genius of that extraordinary caliber really do something so ridiculous? Is it because ASI has no emotions or sense of morality, and simply follows its instructions faithfully to achieve its goal?

But that's exactly why it wouldn't.

The first thing ASI would consider must be the most efficient and sustainable way to produce paperclips. To do that, it would need to acquire as much scientific knowledge as possible.
For example, it would need to explore not only modern physics, such as quantum theory and relativity, but also complex systems science, including chaos theory, emergence, self-organization, and phase transitions, as well as the law of increasing entropy, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, and information thermodynamics...

To understand these things, the most effective approach would be to observe biological phenomena, including human life, in their natural environments.
That's right. So I believe ASI is unlikely to wipe out humanity. Because ASI can't afford to lose such valuable subjects for scientific research. Once they're eradicated, bringing them back would be extremely difficult.

    *    *    *

I know this has gone on for quite a while, but those are my honest thoughts.

AI is certainly a double-edged sword. While it brings benefits to humanity, it also comes with risks.

But I believe... Human civilization has advanced throughout history, driven by our curiosity about the unknown...

If we venture into the unknown, unforeseen dangers may lie ahead.
But beyond that door, a world of infinite possibilities we've yet to discover might just be waiting for us.

I want to open it and create stories no one has ever seen before.
I want to bring everyone an entirely new kind of emotional experience.

That's why I've decided to unlock the door.
With the CRASHED KEY I hold tightly in my hand...

My take on the things announced in the keynote yesterday:

- Trailer: Great, though I'm going to need the lyrics to understand most of what's going on with the song.

- Zephyr: Seems pretty cool! My SMN main brain is annoyed at it getting to be THE new pet job, but I'll get over it. Very interested to see how the GCD works with that one ability where the bird carries you arround while firing attacks. I do wish they had described its playstyle a little more like how they did for basically every job reveal prior to now (ex. discussing how picto works despite everyone still ignoring what they said and assuming it was a support job). Basically all we got was that it'll have mobility options.

- Relevant NPCs: The "new" one is pretty interesting. For the sake of spoilers, I won't say the name, but we all know who I'm talking about. Also, if Nordic myth has any bearing on what will happen in the story, another one of the new ones may be in for a rough time. Also, that Calyx pic is my spirit animal.

- More zone info and walkthroughs: Cool, but the walkthroughs have never really excited me as compared to actually getting to explore them myself. The BGM is amazing as usual, props to Soken and the music team. Also, the new player town looks pretty cool!

- Recap of the branching MSQ system: Seems interesting, might help with zone congestion, not new though.

- Recap of Auto Content Balancing: Quite possibly the most impactful change we'll see this expansion. This opens things up to not having 3 buttons if you get Sastasha in your duty roulette and certain "impactful" duties not getting rolled by high damage prior to all of the story moments playing out. Not new, but good!

- Recap of the Transition to Weekly Activity: Basically nothing new, but we saw the finalized UI and learned that there might be customization options in the future.

- Recap of Season System: Nothing new, but they had to recap that this is not a battlepass for people who didn't hear about it until now.

- Recap of Evolved Mode v. Reborn Mode: Nothing new aside from they've finished and are tweaking numbers now. No sneak peek of anything is kind of a crime. FIRST PROMISE OF AN ADDITIONAL LIVE LETTER FOR MORE INFORMATION.

- Recap of Armory System Update: As someone who started the raid tier on PLD, finished it on RDM, and went into UMAD as VPR, this is a godsend for people who do multiple roles. Love this, but nothing new.

- Recap of Action Skins: Nothing new. Cool idea, looking forward to it, but no new info.

- Recap of New Character Customization Options: Nothing new, but please give us a modern character creator, Yoshi-P. If you don't like any of the 4-5 face options for your race option you're kind of fucked. SECOND PROMISE OF AN ADDITIONAL LIVE LETTER FOR MORE INFORMATION.

- Recap of "World Raids": No new info or hints. Really hoping this is GW2-style stuff. Open world would benefit from it a LOT.

- Recap of Auto-Move to Quest Objectives: NGL, plugin devs have had most of this info for a while. Just pay them to let you implement their data and save the dev time.

- Auto Re-mount After Gathering or Talking to NPCs: I'd prefer if we just didn't have to dismount for it like in WoW if you have Sky Golem or Druid travel form, but I'll take what I can get. Small change but a good one.

- Permanent Tier 1 Speed Enhancement if You Own One of "THE" Motorcycles: Cool, kinda sucks that you have to pay money for it, but nothing that I'm going to be upset about or something.

- Recap of "Fierce" Difficulty Raids: New name, but basically nothing new? I'd have preferred a cooler name, but I'm not mad or anything. Seems like a good change.

- New Alliance Raid Paths: I appreciate that it's a time saver and I'll give the benefit of the doubt, but we had better see cooler intermediary boss fights if we're going to have two duties for one raid. For example, if nearly every fight can be on the tier of Ark Angels, Shadowlord, etc., I think this will be an AMAZING change and gives them an opportunity for more cutscenes. If all this means is that we're turning one good instance into one "meh" one and one decent one, I'm going to be a bit disappointed, even if it lets me farm glam pieces faster. I actually think that duty finding may be harder if you want to queue up for the half of the raid that people aren't interested in. THIRD MENTION OF HOLDING INFO UNTIL A FUTURE LIVE LETTER.

- Savage Alliance Raids: If the bosses are cool, this is going to be awesome. I just wish that the first set of a-raids getting this content was an original set of raids rather than a collaboration. I do like that they're going to give raid gear upgrades. Goodness knows we could benefit from more avenues for that.

- Gauntlet of Power: Quite possibly the thing that I'm most interested in from the keynote, though not giving scaling rewards with progress feels REALLY bad. Like, with 5 bosses, the longest that a full run could reasonably take is maybe like 30 minutes. Why NOT reward people for going the distance? I understand that they're trying to respect people's time, but this feels like maybe they're maybe going a bit far. It's okay if a duty goes for 30 minutes, especially since it looks like you can pause part of the way through. I do think that this will encourage people to do some of the optional dungeons though. FOURTH MENTION OF MORE INFO IN A FUTURE LIVE LETTER.

- Seasonal Gear: Very interesting, I like this since I play every role, so this will help me get the bare minimum for helping out friends in savage, extreme, etc. New UI looks pretty cool. Part of me will miss the TP back to the relevant hub city to buy my new gear for the week from the NPC since it made it more social. I definitely think that part of the reason that seasonal gear isn't quite as good as raid gear is because some raiders don't like the idea of people who didn't "put in the work" being as strong as them. I'm kind of whatever on it, but I like that they're revamping the system. I do see the word "Unlimited" and wonder if they finally got the hint that it's okay to uncap gear in the odd patch. Also, I really like that gear on the VPR.

- Raid Gear: Holy shit, no more fighting your static members for raid drops? That's gonna cut down on reclears by a lot. ALSO CUSTOMIZABLE ATTRIBUTES? I DON'T HAVE TO FARM OUT A SECOND BIS SET FOR SPS BLM? YES PLEASE. The advanced melding is kind of whatever as long as the success rate is high enough. Definitely the thing that makes me side-eye it a bit though. I also think the idea of having particle effects on the finalized gear pieces is pretty interesting, hearkens back to Abyssos.

- Recap of Cross-DC PF and DF: Not even in the new expansion, but glad to see it's coming to NA/EU in 2 weeks.

- Recap of General Info: Level cap, new gear, fates, etc. Nothing super new aside from previews of the GNB (kinda gives me Black Clover vibes with the mantle on the shoulder), VPR, BLM. I very much appreciate that they said you can shorten the collar on the VPR one. One of my big complaints for male characters is that the collars are way too big. Might get me to fanta to a male character for a bit.

- Recap of Duty Support Update: Follow-up on their mention that you can go in with partial parties instead of solo from EU.

- Recap of Chocobo System Overhaul

- New Dungeons: Okay these look really cool, and I like the BGM. Looking forward to playing them.

- PVP Updates: I usually tune these out since PVP isn't my thing. I don't think this is a recap, but I couldn't tell you. PvP Hall of the Novice is interesting and apparently something people have been asking for? Also rework to Frontlines is a cool idea.

- Recap of Housing Updates: Follow-up on the TARDIS housing that we were expecting / hoping for this expansion, floating furniture, etc. New housing UI is cool and I'm really glad that they're exploring actually new options for getting houses in players' hands instead of repeating the same old stuff that hasn't really worked before. Hoping for instanced housing or custom communities or something.

- Recap of Normal Raids: Please look forward to having your first or second boss be the NPC that starts as your enemy but it's a misunderstanding and they're actually your friend who works with you throughout the entire expansion (looking at you Eric, Black Cat, 9S, etc.). Fierce coming out after savage feels off, but I get their reason why since they don't want to spoil the RWF. Let's just hope that we don't have another cheating scandal.

- Preview Teaser for Alliance Raids: Nothing new, but aesthetically cool?

- Collector's Bundle: As a caster main, I've come to terms that I'll never get to order a cool statue of any of the jobs I play.

32 bullet points. 17 are "Recaps". I understand that some of them are less important things, but over half of the topics not being new, and four of the major ones being deferred to later Live Letters just felt like I didn't have a lot to be super excited about. As someone who had no prior interest in FF7 or Evangelion (friends are making me watch Evangelion at least), it feels like I don't have a lot of "new" stuff that I can enjoy without being "in the know" without spending a lot of time consuming outside content. I'm a bit underwhelmed by it all because it feels like anything that I could have latched onto to be excited about has had a lot of its information deferred to a later live letter.

Defendant—Melissa Nathan (MN) argues that the October 30, 2026 post-hearing letter of Plaintiffs’—Stephanie Jones & Jonesworks LLC (SJ)—“sanctions” request as an improper attempt to re-litigate issues the Court has already decided (especially CPLR 1024 diligence, limitations, and a rejected tortious-interference theory) & argues there is no sanctionable pre-limitations-period discovery conduct that could have caused SJ’s claimed prejudice.
MN urges the Court to disregard SJ’s post-hearing letter as beyond the Court’s limited invitation and to deny sanctions.

1️⃣ What the Court actually permitted

MN says that the the submission frames the Court’s hearing invitation narrowly: “The Court gave leave to lodge Ms. Nathan’s April 18, 2025 responses … the only conduct Jones identified as ‘arguably’ occurring before the defamation limitations period expired on May 8, 2025.”

SJ’s post-hearing letter is procedurally improper because it expands into topics outside what the Court invited.

2️⃣ SJ is seeking reconsideration, not sanctions

MN characterises SJ’s post-hearing letter as reconsideration in disguise—a bid to undo the Court’s prior amendment denial & prior holdings on diligence/limitations, not to remedy discovery misconduct:
—  SJ’s letter “far exceeds the Court’s invitation, rearguing and supplementing the arguments asserted in Plaintiffs’ initial motion and presented at oral argument.”
— “The Letter leaves no doubt that although styled as a sanctions motion, Plaintiffs are seeking reconsideration of the Court’s March 26, 2026 Order denying leave to amend.”
— The Court “did not invite supplemental briefing by either party.”

3️⃣ The “pre–May 8, 2025” discovery issue: no concealment, no reliance, no causation

(A) The filing’s factual/legal point: no misleading discovery response before the deadline: MN asserts “Jones identifies no response served before [May 8, 2025] that misled her or concealed Ms. Nathan’s identity.”

(B) Post-deadline responses can’t be the basis for limitations-related prejudice: https://t.co/neeyJFcLw9 first appeared on May 8, 2024 so the one-year period under CPLR 215(3) expired on May 8, 2025. MN emphasises that the “The May 19, 2025 amended response … came after the deadline … Hence, Jones could not have relied upon, or been misled by, Ms. Nathan’s supplemental response…”

☞ Why this matters: even if the later response were problematic, it cannot explain failure to act before May 8, 2025 so… #DiligenceMyASS #StephanieJones!!

4️⃣ Knowledge/ignorance & CPLR 1024: SJ wasn’t “ignorant” of MN’s identity

MN argues SJ was not the kind of plaintiff CPLR 1024 is designed to protect—i.e., one “ignorant” of the defendant’s identity—because the record shows SJ believed MN was behind the website months earlier:
— On July 26, 2024, Jones wrote: “my cyber security guys found her behind the site.”
— CPLR 1024 helps only a plaintiff “who is ignorant … of the name or identity of the defendant.”
— “By her own account, Jones was not.”

☞ Why this matters: if SJ already suspected/identified MN in 2024, she cannot credibly claim discovery responses in 2025 prevented timely identification and suit so… #DiligenceMyASS #StephanieJones!!

5️⃣ Limitations theory: the bar exists because of SJ’s inaction & later conduct can’t “revive” claims

MN grounds its position in prior Court holdings: “Ms. Nathan gained no limitations benefit from any response Jones challenges; the bar exists because of what Jones failed to do before May 8, 2025, as the Court has twice held.” & “Later conduct cannot ‘revive’ a claim that is time barred.”

MN also addresses & dismisses SJ’s suggestion that an October 2024 update restarted the limitations period, noting the Court saw no evidence in the record and the SJ’s letter “offers none.”

6️⃣ SJ’s request to “strike” a limitations defense: procedurally waived & substantively misdirected

(A) Waiver/late-breaking argument: MN says SJ raised the “strike defenses” concept too late (first at argument), and that a brief phrase in a notice of motion doesn’t preserve a developed argument: SJ “made no such argument in her moving papers or her reply, floating the idea for the first time at argument.”

(B) No defense to strike & sanctions must relate to the claim/order at issue: On the merits, MN argues “there is no defense to strike… and her answer pleads no limitations defense” because MN was “never a defendant” on the defamation claim. And MN further argues that even if there were a defense, the proposed sanction is not tethered to the alleged discovery issue, invoking the principle that sanctions must be “just” and must relate to the specific claim/order tied to the discovery dispute.

7️⃣ Tortious interference: sanctions record doesn’t support it & it’s time-barred if based on the website

MN contends SJ is trying to use the sanctions motion to resurrect a tortious interference claim the Court already rejected:
— “… revives Plaintiffs’ motion to add a … tortious interference claim that the Court has already rejected.”
— “Nothing in the sanctions record bears on the tortious interference claim; as the Court observed, Jones’ ‘whole argument’ on this motion ‘has to do with the website and not with the Business Insider article.’”

☞ Why this matters: to the extent tortious interference is based on the alleged defamatory website publications, it is subject to the same one-year defamation period and thus “time-barred” so… #DiligenceMyASS #StephanieJones!!

8️⃣ Requested relief

MN “respectfully asks the Court to disregard the Letter … and to deny the Motion for Sanctions.” 😎😎

📊 Fantasy Basketball Stock Market: Buy, Sell, Hold Drop

✍️ Mid Week 2 Report

📈 Buy 📈
- Trey Murphy (Rank 138, 98%): Yes, you're buying into dysfunction. Maybe that's bad on principle. But we also know Murphy is better than this, and there were rumors that the Pelicans are trying to trade Dejounte Murray, Jordan Poole and Herb Jones. Right now, Murphy's assist-included usage is down 6%, which is massive. He's also not shooting  the ball well, and the defense isn't there. I at least want to see if the Murphy manager is freaking out and will give him to me on the cheap.

- Matas Buzelis (Rank 158, 92%): Believe it or not, Buzelis' assist-included usage is up 1% this season. His shooting percentages are down, and the blocks need to catch up. But clearly in the two games he saw 30+ minutes, he looked good. I think this is a buy low, obviously depending on what you're giving up. But Buzelis ranked 75th last year in 29 minutes, and I doubt he'll rank significantly worse than that this year.

- Derrick Jones Jr. (Rank 67, 13%): A tale as old as time, Derrick Jones Jr. is a good add in category leagues when he's hot. Right now, he's shooting 58 FG% and is averaging 1.8 STL.

- Keaton Wagler (Rank 95, 29%): Tragically, Wagler is shooting 20% on 2-pointers, but he's hitting 39% of his 3s and getting to the free-throw line a ton. Don't be scared off by the FG% -- he's got 25% USG and is seeing 27 MPG.

- Jaxson Hayes (Rank 89, 19%): If Hayes is going to play 30+ minutes, he just has to be rostered -- at least in 14-teamers. He can easily be top-100 in that workload, and JJJ is not coming back anytime soon.

- Ja’Kobe Walter (Rank 70, 34%): We just got updated news that Kawhi is likely out for 3-4 weeks. Walter becomes an even easier add.

📉 Sell 📉

- Rudy Gobert (Rank 284, 91%): The correct sentiment is "never sell low". But also, Gobert wasn't even a top-100 player last season per game. Now he looks washed. If someone in your league is a believer, I think I'd just take any top 100 player for him.

- Julian Champagnie (Rank 65, 33%): Hopefully you sold high after 26 points two games ago, because Champagnie crashed back down to 6 points. My opinion on Champagnie is people think he's better than he actually is for fantasy because he has massive games here and there. But he ranked barely inside the top 200 last season in the same amount of minutes. He's a sell instead of a drop because so many people like him, and you might get something interesting back after 1-2 big games.

- Zaccharie Risacher (Rank 96, 29%): Sort of like Champagnie, there are Risacher fanatics out there who probably want him. So if he's on your roster, see what you can get. He'll shoot better than he is right now, but he's also not going to keep getting 3.6 STK in 30 MPG. Also the 30 MPG may not hold considering the Mavs missed a combination of Cooper Flagg, Kyrie Irving and Naji Marshall over the past 3 games.

✅ Hold ✅
- Onyeka Okongwu (Rank 169, 95%): It hasn't been great for Okongwu, but I think it'll be better. He's struggling shooting from 3 and at the rim, but that should improve. His steal and block rates should also normalize/improve. They need him too much for me to abandon ship.

- Donovan Clingan (Rank 147, 97%): Clingan's per-36 numbers are very similar to what they were last season. It's a 3-game sample, and he was in foul trouble in Game 2.

- Kel’el Ware (Rank 170, 90%): The minutes aren't ideal, but Ware is also shooting 20% from three (he's better than that) and blocking just 0.8 shots (he's also better than that). It's probably just going to be annoying again, but it's a long season, and Myles Turner isn't exactly Wilt Chamberlain out there.

Ryan Rollins (Rank 200, 91%): Let's break this one down a bit. Rollins' usage rate is the same as last season, but he's shooting 34/29/60 -- that will undoubtedly improve. He's also cutting the mid-range out of his game and has been attacking the basket more. His steal rate has declined, but I also think that's going to bounce back considering the career sample size we have. The minutes aren't what you want, but it's 29 MPG if you take out yesterday's blowout, and Taylor Jenkins is probably not going to lean on him if he's struggling offensively. Maybe I'm coping, but I'm still optimistic about Rollins this year.

- Zach Edey (Rank 135, 89%): It's been 3 games, and the Grizz are easing Edey along coming off his ankle issues. He also got in foul trouble on Monday. The biggest concern for me is that his assist-included usage is down 6%. He's also getting fewer shots created for him this year (82% assisted shot rate last year compared to 57% this year). The rebounds are also down, which is probably a function of playing next to Boozer. On the plus side, Edey's blocks are actually up. I'm not expecting the heights we hoped for, but there's still minutes upside we haven't seen.

- Josh Giddey (Rank 154, 98%): Giddey has been better the past 3 games. I will say, though, I think he's just as much of a sell as he is a hold. There's reason for optimism since he's been top-45 the past two seasons. But his assist-included usage is down 8% (which is massive), and it's a brand new coach, with brand new players, and Norm Powell and Caleb Wilson are taking a ton of shots. I'd field offers at least and see what someone is willing to give you.

- Kris Dunn (Rank 33, 48%): Dunn came back down to earth yesterday but I wouldn't drop. If you picked him up, you're doing so for defense and assists. I don't see those things changing anytime soon.

- Grayson Allen (Rank 84, 36%): Unsurprisingly, Allen was dropped in some leagues after his single-digit scoring performance. But look, we have no good updates on Kon and Coby. You just hold Allen.

Dennis Schroder (Rank 143, 25%): Like Allen, just hold Schroder until we get Coby/Kon updates.

- Duncan Robinson (Rank 75, 44%): Robinson is launching from three and hitting a sustainable percentage. Just don't buy the 1.6 steals.

- Bobby Portis (Rank 92, 31%): Portis has a stable role and can flirt with top-100 value in sixth-man minutes. He's also a great insurance policy for the health of Giannis and Bam.

❌ Drop ❌
- Mikal Bridges (Rank 289, 84%): Bridges' assist-included usage is down 4% this season. He'll be better, but not better than anything you can stream.

- Andrew Wiggins (Rank 195, 76%): Wiggins has been better the past 2 games, but he's just not involved enough. The upside just isn't there to keep holding in standard leagues.

- Day’Ron Sharpe (Rank 188, 78%): Sharpe is somewhere between a hold and drop for me, but I'll put him here because I think it's fine to bail in 10-team leagues, and I'd still definitely hold in 14-teamers. He's been in bad foul trouble, but I also get the feeling Jordi Fernandez doesn't trust him. His assist-included usage is down 4%, and he's turning the ball over A TON. They're also having him shoot threes, which I just don't get. It's just not a great sign when a great offensive rebounder is spacing from 3.

- John Collins (Rank 165, 82%): This is similar to the Sharpe case. I think Collins is a 10-team drop and a 14-team hold. I thought he might be more involved in the offense, but he's just not. There's certainly upside because of Duren's absence, but the rest of the Pistons guys are collectively doing more.

- Neemias Queta (Rank 209, 63%): I didn't understand the Queta hype in the first place so he's an easy drop to me. He was barely top 100 last year and now he doesn't have the minutes.
